files.name: t1_lib.c

notes.4: `p` points at the start of the received heartbeat record; `pl` will point at its payload.
notes.10: Reads the 1-byte heartbeat message type and advances the pointer.
notes.11: `n2s` reads a 2-byte big-endian length from the request into `payload` — this value is attacker-supplied.
notes.12: `pl` now points at the payload bytes within the received request buffer.
notes.20: Allocates the response buffer, sized from the attacker's claimed `payload` length.
notes.24: `s2n` writes the 2-byte payload length into the response.
notes.25: Copies `payload` bytes starting at `pl` into the response.
notes.29: Sends the assembled response back to the peer.

options.label: `OPENSSL_malloc` can return NULL for a huge length, so `bp` is dereferenced on a null pointer
options.whyWrong: Allocation failure is a separate, lesser issue. The disclosure happens because the copy reads from the request buffer beyond what was received.

options.label: `payload` is attacker-controlled and never checked against the real record length, so `memcpy` reads past the received data into adjacent process memory
`RAND_pseudo_bytes` is not cryptographically secure, so the padding is predictable
options.whyWrong: Padding quality is irrelevant to the leak; the response echoes memory that was never part of the request.

options.label: Reject requests whose claimed length exceeds the record, and drop 0-length
Cap the payload length at a fixed maximum
options.whyWrong: Clamping to a constant still lets the request claim a length larger than the actual record, so the memcpy reads past the received data. The length must be checked against the real record length, not a fixed cap.

options.label: Zero the response buffer before copying
options.whyWrong: This addresses the destination, not the source. The leak is the over-read from `pl` (the request buffer), which is copied into the response regardless of how the buffer was initialised.

options.label: Use the returned length from a checked read of the payload
options.diff:
-    memcpy(bp, pl, payload);
+    memcpy(bp, pl, strlen((char *)pl));
options.whyWrong: `strlen` on binary TLS data is meaningless and itself reads out of bounds until it finds a NUL. It does not bound the copy to the record and introduces a second over-read.

training.exploit: Send a heartbeat request with a tiny actual payload but a claimed `payload` length of 65535. The server allocates a 64 KB response and `memcpy` copies 64 KB starting at `pl`, scooping up whatever follows the request in memory — private keys, session cookies, other users' plaintext — and returns it. Repeat to walk large swaths of server memory, no authentication required.

hints.line: Find where bytes are copied using a length the client supplied.
hints.bugClass: Nothing is written out of bounds — but something is read that shouldn't be.
hints.why: Compare `payload` against how many bytes actually arrived.
hints.fix: Validate the claimed length against `s->s3->rrec.length` before copying.

writeup.summary: `payload` is a 16-bit length read straight from the heartbeat request with `n2s`, but the code never checks it against the actual length of the record received (`s->s3->rrec.length`). An attacker sends a tiny heartbeat that *claims* a 65535-byte payload; `memcpy(bp, pl, payload)` then copies 64 KB starting at the request buffer, sweeping up whatever adjacent process memory follows it — private keys, session data, other users' requests — and sends it back in the response. This is an out-of-bounds read (information disclosure), not a write-based overflow. The real fix adds two guards: discard records too short to even hold a heartbeat, and reject any request whose claimed length plus padding exceeds the record. This is Heartbleed.
